newsitem.title: UK: EU ruling on Saunders puts UK laws in spotlight.
newsitem.headline: EU ruling on Saunders puts UK laws in spotlight.

text.p: Britain's ability to prosecute fraud is under scrutiny but should not be undermined, fraud experts said on Tuesday after a European Court of Human Rights ruling in favour of former Guinness Plc chairman Ernest Saunders.

The Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) said in a statement that it would study the findings of the EU court "to see what implications there are for UK company regulation and criminal prosecutions,"
And the Serious Fraud Office (SFO), which prosecutes major frauds, said it would fight any attempt to overturn Saunders' 1990 fraud conviction.

The European Court ruled earlier that DTI statements should not have been used in evidence against him. Under the 1985 Companies Act, DTI inspectors can require suspects to answer their questions and can threaten them with fines or imprisonment of up to two years if they fail to comply.

The SFO, which was set up in 1988, has similar powers -- known as "Section 2 powers" -- in its own right but cannot use the evidence obtained in court, unless it is used as a rebuttal to later contradictory statements made by a defendant. "The issue is whether DTI transcripts can be used in a criminal trial," one fraud specialist said.
While lawyers and fraud experts generally agreed the European ruling meant such transcripts were unlikely to be able to be used in future, some said it would have little impact.
"I think it (the European ruling) has a very limited application for future fraud trials," Martyn Bridges, of accountancy firm Deloitte Touche told Reuters.

Bridges stressed that the SFO's Section 2 powers were "a totally different concept" to those exercised by the DTI under the Companies Act, adding that the SFO's powers were widely used for information gathering.
This differed from the Saunders case where DTI transcripts of interviews had been used as evidence against him.

But while Saunders said he was delighted with the Strasbourg court's judgement and the trial had been unfair, the DTI pointed out in its statement that the Court of Human Rights had "declined to speculate on the question of whether the outcome of Mr Saunders' trial would have been any different if the compulsory statements had not been used."
The court did order Britain to pay Saunders, who was sacked as chairman of British drinks giant Guinness in 1987, 75,000 pounds ($124,900) in legal costs, although it refused him compensation.

Saunders, now 61, was convicted of 12 counts including false accounting and theft for inflating Guinness' share price to help its 1986 takeover of whisky group Distillers Plc prevail against rival bidder Argyll Plc.
One of these counts was dropped on his first appeal in 1991 when his original five-year prison sentence was shortened to two-and-a-half years. He eventually served 10 months.

The SFO currently has 250 cases in which proceedings are under way and transcripts have been used, and 240 of them relate to the DTI. But fraud specialists said that any changes to the legislation would not be retrospective.
But Tuesday's ruling could lead to actions by the others in the "Guinness Four" convicted with Saunders -- businessmen Gerald Ronson and Jack Lyons, and financier Tony Parnes.

The DTI currently has 340 cases going through the British courts where some of the evidence obtained has been gained through its use of compulsion powers. But the vast majority of these relate to company insolvency rather than insider dealing.
Britain's opposition Labour party said there was still concern over the way some high profile City cases had been handled by the SFO and the DTI.

"This ruling raises new questions about whether DTI inspectors can use their powers under the legislation to tackle City problems in the future and whether the present legislation is adequate," Labour's Treasury spokesman Michael O'Brian said.
